summary:
Egypt's immigration law gives the Ministry of Interior broad authority to refuse entry to, or order the removal of, anyone deemed to disturb public order or morality. Cairo 52's study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that statute and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents from 2018 to 2022, and finds the power applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans in cases where no charge was ever upheld. Removal requires neither a conviction nor any offence.

No penal provision in Egypt names homosexual conduct. Prosecution instead runs through the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961: Cairo 52 reported on 24 January 2024 that the Economic Courts have moved from de-facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of that statute. Court of Cassation interpretations from the 1970s had already removed the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners suffices to sustain a charge. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records vague public-morality and debauchery provisions used for arrests carrying prison sentences.

Policing of dating applications is documented. A BBC investigation, "How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps", found officers running entrapment operations through those apps, with victims describing blackmail and arrests. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents entrapment through fake accounts on LGBT dating apps and websites, transgender women in particular as targets, and records violations continuing inside police stations.

Custody carries documented physical abuse. Bedayaa's briefing of February 2023 records rising arrests of gay and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations and authorities turning a blind eye. Human Rights Watch's "In a Time of Torture" (29 February 2004) documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings justified by sexual orientation, with defendants' own testimony. After the September 2017 rainbow-flag incident, at least 84 people were arrested between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. A December 2014 police raid on a public bathhouse arrested around 26 men, who were later acquitted. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labour, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site. The most recent dated arrest-and-forced-examination incident in the sources cited here is from 2017; no later instance is documented.

Legal gender recognition is being actively closed. Cairo 52 reported on 12 December 2024 that a new Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide shuts the loophole in Civil Status Law 143/1994 that had let transgender Egyptians correct gender markers through governorate committees.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination. Outright International's overview, updated 12 March 2026, records no legal protection on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics; Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing likewise records the absence of any anti-discrimination policy or law.

Healthcare access is restricted on identity grounds. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle (6 January 2025) states that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health, that barriers to equitable health services persist since the previous cycle, and that gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare is pervasive.

Personal and family law is governed by the religious law of the person's recognised religion (Islam, Coptic Orthodox Christianity), and Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. Where a relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status and becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.
tangentialFactors:
Official incitement has accompanied documented arrests. After the September 2017 rainbow-flag incident, television hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against LGBT people; Moussa published the personal information of flag-raisers, feeding a wave of arrests. In December 2014 television presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police on the bathhouse raid. In January 2019 host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his programme. In 2009 the newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed over a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution.

Social hostility is measured but undated in the source: Pew Research Center is cited as finding that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling is described as showing only minority support for LGBT rights. Because the inventory gives no year for that survey, it should be read as background rather than a current reading.

Visibility work produced no legislative change. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible, and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia had gone viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, without any resulting legal reform. Egyptian political parties and human-rights NGOs do not express public support for LGBT rights.

Displacement is documented at individual level. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the 2017 incident, fled the country, was granted asylum abroad and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals have left the country under social and political pressure.

The structural comparison matters for expectation-setting: Egypt is a jurisdiction where the penal code does not name homosexual conduct, yet prosecutions proceed through morality and sex-work provisions with prison sentences attached. The absence of an explicit statute does not indicate absence of exposure.
localsOnly:
The national media regulator issued an order in 2017 preventing "the appearance of the homosexuals" or the promotion of their slogans in media output.

In August 2018 legislation placed any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and potential prosecution under media laws, which raises the exposure of prominent LGBT Egyptians and anyone documenting their lives.

In 2013 the government of the day charged television comedian Bassem Youssef with propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity.

Gender-nonconforming expression carries a specifically stigmatised label: the term historically describing male cross-dressing dancers is used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively through stereotyping and defamation.

Residents have no anti-discrimination recourse in employment, services or healthcare, and Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing documents detention conditions alongside that absence of a legal remedy.
outOfScopeNotes:
No border, immigration or airport screening protocol specific to trans travellers is documented in the sources assembled here: there is no sourced account of document-marker flagging, targeted anatomy inspection or a binder- or prosthesis-triggered secondary search at Egyptian points of entry. Whether an amended or unamended gender marker on a foreign passport affects entry is unresolved and not sourced.

The BBC investigation into dating-app entrapment and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights police documentation carry no publication date in the inventory, so their currency cannot be fixed.

The Pew Research Center acceptance figure has no year attached in the inventory and cannot be dated here.

The legal effect of the 12 December 2024 Ministry of Interior directive is unresolved: the sources do not state whether it has been challenged in court, whether transitional cases were grandfathered, or how it is being applied to foreign documents.

No trans-specific homicide or violence rate with a denominator appears in the inventory, so no comparative risk figure is given. The arrest totals cited (at least 84 people between 25 September and the end of November 2017; around 26 men in December 2014) are raw counts for single operations and are not ranked against other jurisdictions, since raw counts track population rather than risk.

Several items in the inventory derive from a Wikipedia country overview whose own citations were not verified here, including the media-regulator order, the 5,000-follower rule, and the individual prosecutions of journalists and broadcasters.

Recency: the most recent dated arrest-and-forced-examination incident documented in these sources is from 2017, and the most recent deportation cases run to 2022. No later instance is documented, which is an absence of documentation and not evidence that the practice has stopped.
